title: Technical deep dive: multi-region routing & failover
summary: Deep dive on multi-region routing and failover design for latency and DR. Covered policy routing, regional capacity, fallback models, KV cache behavior across regions, VPC/on-prem constraints, and draft DR playbooks. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run bench, share routing playbook and security docs, customer to provide regional qps and compliance constraints.
next_steps: Redwood: Share multi-region routing playbook PDF and diagram (Lena) by 2026-04-24
Redwood: Run failover benchmark across us-west/us-east/eu (Marcus) and send results by 2026-04-27

Schedule follow-up pilot planning call for POC scoping week of 2026-04-28
action_items: Lena Park: Share routing/playbook + diagram PDF by 2026-04-24
Marcus Chen: Kick off synthetic failover benchmark, upload results to shared sheet by 2026-04-27

transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. We have about an hour, technical deep dive on multi-region routing and failover. Marcus will lead the topology part. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Aisha Thompson: Aisha here, CTO at Nimbus. Diego and Markus also on.
[00:18] Diego Rivera: Diego, SRE. Hey.
[00:20] Markus Lee: Markus, ML.
[00:22] Lena Park: Great. Marcus?
[00:24] Marcus Chen: Yeah, hi all. Quick agenda: policy routing, regional capacity, cache behavior (KV cache), batching/quantization fallbacks, VPC considerations, then draft DR playbook steps.
[00:38] Markus Lee: Sounds good. We're mainly worried about latency spikes in eu-west during peak and cross-region failover that doesn't blow up cost.
[00:45] Marcus Chen: Right. High-level, we support three routing modes: latency-first, cost-aware, and sticky-region. Latency-first routes to the lowest p99 latency region that has available capacity. Cost-aware favors cheaper instance pools or quantized variants, sticky-region keeps affinity to a home region for cache locality.
[01:05] Aisha Thompson: That sticky thing is important for us, we do session affinity and we rely on warmed KV caches, otherwise responses regress.
[01:12] Marcus Chen: Exactly. KV cache is per-model-host; when you fail over to a different region you lose local KV warm entries unless you use Redis-based shared KV, but that increases cross-region RTTs. So tradeoffs: 1) prefer sticky-region with fast warm-up strategies, 2) async pre-warm on failover, or 3) use prefix-sharing and accept a cold-start latency hit.
[01:36] Diego Rivera: How big is that hit typically? We saw 200-300ms per request during our internal tests but want numbers for real traffic.
[01:44] Marcus Chen: It varies by sequence length and KV size; for typical chat workloads we've measured p50 delta of ~80-150ms and p99 delta up to 800ms when KV is cold, especially for long context. We'll share the benchmark sheet. Note: quantized models can behave differently with KV caching due to different kernel execution paths, sometimes a bit faster token throughput but slightly higher variance.
[02:10] Lena Park: Also worth noting policy-level fallbacks: if region A is saturated, we can do graceful degradation: route a percentage to region B, route some to a smaller/faster quantized model, and keep a small steady flow to the primary for sticky sessions. That avoids mass cold starts in a single region.
[02:28] Aisha Thompson: If we route to a smaller model for cost reasons, how do we measure quality regression? Markus?
[02:33] Markus Lee: We usually define a set of prompt families and run automatic evals for BLEU/ROUGE-style heuristics or embedding similarity thresholds. For Nimbus, acceptable threshold is 95% embedding similarity for top-critical flows. Anything below triggers rollback.
[02:45] Marcus Chen: Good to capture. One of our routing knobs is automatic rollback if quality metrics drop during an A/B routing period. We also support percentage rollouts and can pin customers to dedicated pools.
[02:58] Diego Rivera: For VPC/on-prem, we have an air-gapped region for regulated data. How does failover work if the private region can't reach public regions?
[03:08] Marcus Chen: In private deployments we can configure replication policies: either full private-only (no external fallback) or private-first with encrypted egress to Redwood Dedicated fallback via a peered path. For strict air-gapped setups, failover is local only — so you need capacity planning and cross-zone redundancy inside your datacenter.
[03:28] Aisha Thompson: For compliance, we need audit logs for every routing decision. Do you emit trace events?
[03:33] Lena Park: Yes, all routing decisions are logged to the observability pipeline. We can show sample audit entries (we'll include in the playbook). Logs include decision reason (latency/capacity/quota), model variant used, region, and request id.
[03:45] Diego Rivera: Nice.
[03:47] Markus Lee: Let's talk DR playbook. What are the steps you recommend?
[03:50] Marcus Chen: Draft DR playbook (high level): 1) Detection: anomaly in p99 or region health (we use both active probes and passive telemetry). 2) Containment: spillover by policy (e.g., 30% to failover region, 70% to primary) while starting cache pre-warm jobs. 3) Stabilize: incrementally increase traffic while monitoring quality/regression signals. 4) Rollback/evacuate: if quality drops or cost overruns, revert routes and scale down; or if primary remains unhealthy, promote failover region and notify stakeholders. 5) Recovery: reverse steps, drain traffic back to primary, and perform postmortem.
[04:25] Aisha Thompson: How automated is this vs manual? We want automation but with guardrails.
[04:30] Lena Park: Playbooks can be automated with SLO-based triggers plus manual approval gates for risky changes (e.g. model fallback beyond X% of traffic). We'll attach default thresholds but they can be tuned.
[04:40] Diego Rivera: Can we simulate failover? We need a safe way to run chaos tests.
[04:44] Marcus Chen: Yes, we run canary failovers in staging, and we can run shadow traffic and synthetic probes. We'll give you a checklist for a chaos test: regional throttle, induced p99 spike, and monitor cache warm-up impact. We'll run an initial synthetic test as part of the POC.
[05:00] Markus Lee: Regarding latency tail, do you use connection draining or immediate cutover? Connection draining helps preserve cache locality but slows failover.
[05:08] Marcus Chen: We support configurable connection draining windows. Typical recommendation: 60-120s drain to let KV cache TTLs and active sessions finish; if risk unacceptable, you can set lower drain with more pre-warming.
[05:20] Aisha Thompson: Are there tools to estimate cost impact of failover? We have finance constraints.
[05:25] Lena Park: Redwood Optimize includes a cost simulation engine — we can run a what-if for spilling 50% to eu-east on quantized instances vs full unquantized on dedicated. We'll include sample sims.
[05:38] Diego Rivera: On encryption and KMS, if we route across regions, does that expose keys? We're using customer-managed KMS in our VPC.
[05:45] Marcus Chen: We support KMS/HSM integrations. For cross-region fallbacks, keys never leave your control plane in private deployments; for hosted, we can integrate with customer KMS via peered key access or envelope encryption. We'll share the security doc.
[06:00] Markus Lee: A question about KV cache population: can you warm specific user prefixes ahead of failover?
[06:06] Marcus Chen: Yes, we provide pre-warm APIs and batch ingest endpoints to populate KV entries in target region before traffic shifts. That helps reduce p99 spikes. Typical pattern: identify top N sessions by tokens and pre-warm the corresponding prefixes.
[06:20] Lena Park: Also note we have a hybrid option: keep short-lived session state in a global cache (Redis) with region-local LRU for hot keys. That reduces cold-starts at the cost of occasional cross-region reads.
[06:33] Aisha Thompson: That might work. What's the expected latency penalty for cross-region redis reads?
[06:38] Marcus Chen: Usually 30-70ms extra per lookup depending on region pair, plus jitter. If your model is chatty with many KV lookups per request it compounds.
[06:47] Diego Rivera: For batching, does the runtime re-batch when requests reroute to a different region? We want to keep throughput high.
[06:53] Marcus Chen: Yes, runtime supports continuous batching within each region. If you split traffic, batching windows per region might be smaller, reducing GPU efficiency; that's why routing policies try to avoid fragmenting traffic. One mitigation is to route a percentage of similar traffic types together to preserve batching.
[07:10] Markus Lee: Any recommendations for quantization during failover? We worry about quality delta.
[07:15] Marcus Chen: Use quantized variants for non-critical flows or as transitory fallback. Always gate with quality checks. In practice, quantized float16/int8 variants show <3% drop on embedding similarity for most of our models, but specific prompt families can be more sensitive. We'll include recommended thresholds per model in the playbook.
[07:36] Aisha Thompson: Let's talk about alerting and ops runbook items. We want clear pages for SRE.
[07:41] Marcus Chen: We'll provide runbook entries: key metrics to monitor (regional p99, CPU/GPU utilization, queue lengths, model error rates, KV miss rate), triggers for automated steps, and manual escalation contacts. Also we can emit structured events to your pager system.
[07:58] Diego Rivera: On the step where you pre-warm, do you ever get consistency issues between model variants? Like different tokenization?
[08:04] Marcus Chen: Good callout. We recommend standardizing tokenizer and model family for pinned sessions. If you failover to a different ARCH or tokenizer, you can get mismatch. Our routing layer enforces compatibility constraints: only route to model variants with compatible tokenizer and sequence semantics.
[08:20] Lena Park: Aisha, Diego — any other constraints?
[08:23] Aisha Thompson: Data residency: EU PII must stay in EU. We need explicit deny policies for cross-region routing of those requests.
[08:30] Marcus Chen: We support policy tags on requests; you can mark traffic as 'eu-only' and routing honors that. We'll include examples in the playbook.
[08:38] Markus Lee: Cost gating — can we set a global rate cap to prevent failover cost explosion?
[08:42] Marcus Chen: Yes, you can set circuit-breaker caps: total tokens per minute, spend per hour, or per-customer quotas. If breached we can throttle or degrade to cheaper model variants.
[08:54] Lena Park: Ok let's run a quick example: eu-west experiences 60% latency increase and high GPU queues. DR policy triggers: 30% spill to eu-central quantized pool, 20% to us-east full model for sticky sessions, 50% remains with reduced concurrency in eu-west. Pre-warms kick in for top 500 prefixes in eu-central. Monitoring looks at p99, embedding sim, and KV miss rate. If embedding sim drops below 94% we automatically rollback.
[09:24] Diego Rivera: That flow seems reasonable. What about notifications?
[09:27] Marcus Chen: We provide integrated alerts and can send Slack/pager events with playbook step links and decision rationale.
[09:34] Lena Park: Wrap up: we'll share the playbook, the sample audit log format, security doc with KMS details, and a bench sheet for the synthetic failover. Marcus will run initial failover bench and upload results.
[09:46] Aisha Thompson: Thanks. One last question — any limitations for on-prem with older GPUs?
[09:50] Marcus Chen: Older GPUs may not support some kernels or quantization paths; we maintain a compatibility matrix and a recommended baseline (A100/RTX 6000 or equivalent). For older hardware, we recommend Dedicated with small model variants or additional tuning. We'll include the matrix.
[10:07] Markus Lee: Great.
[10:09] Lena Park: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials and schedule the POC planning.
[10:14] Diego Rivera: Thanks.
[10:16] Aisha Thompson: Thanks.
[10:18] Lena Park: End.
